en.title: Seas and coasts
en.summary: Beaches, cliffs and islands, with the language of suggestions and tides.

paragraphs: The coast is a favourite place for holidays and day trips. This lesson describes the coastal landscape and teaches you to suggest plans and talk about safety.

Britain has a long and varied coastline, with sandy beaches, chalk cliffs and rocky bays. The White Cliffs of Dover look across the English Channel to France, and the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland has thousands of stone columns. Australia has the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef in the world. A family plans a day at the seaside.

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: Shall we go to the seaside on Sunday?

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.text: Good idea. Let's take a picnic.

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: The sea is cold, but we can paddle. And we must check the tide times, because it can be dangerous.

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.text: At low tide there's a huge beach, but at high tide it almost disappears.

lines.speaker: Child
lines.text: Can we climb on the rocks?

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: Only if you stay close. Don't go near the edge of the cliffs.

paragraphs: **1. Shall we and let's make suggestions.** They invite agreement. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

We could...We could paddle.

paragraphs: **2. At the seaside and on the coast.** Prepositions of place differ for the area and the point. See Introduction to Grammar: Prepositions and conjunctions.

items: The White Cliffs of Dover look over the English Channel.
The Great Barrier Reef off Australia is the largest coral reef in the world.
The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland has thousands of stone columns.
The tide goes in and out twice a day.

paragraphs: Check the tide table before walking on beaches with rocks. Lifeguards watch many British beaches in summer, and flags show where it is safe to swim.
